status: Original draft classroom material; educator review required before use with real students. Not a validated instrument.
delivery_rules: Treat the teacher_only block as server/teacher content. Never serialize it into student payloads or import the full source into student bundles.
Display order may be shuffled using stable option IDs. Stable IDs preserve scoring across phases.
Identical anchor versions may be compared within matched learners. Fresh recheck items are distinct tasks.
Confidence is optional and is not scored.
Optional explanations require teacher review; absent review is pending, not zero.

modules.title: Choices and what we give up
modules.goal: Identify the next-best alternative given up when making a choice.
modules.success_criterion: I can name the next-best option and explain why it is the opportunity cost.
modules.illustration_direction: Two rounded choice cards connected by a forked path; no correct lifestyle preference implied.

activity.title: The next-best choice
materials: A choice arrow or movable token

steps.teacher_says: Here are library club, football, and a film. For this fictional character the order is library first, football second, film third. Only one can happen.
steps.action: Lay out the three cards in the stated order.

steps.teacher_says: The character chooses library club. Which option is next best? What did they give up?
steps.action: Move the token to the chosen card and point to the next-best card.

steps.teacher_says: A new character prefers film, then library, then football. Does the opportunity cost stay the same? Why?
steps.action: Reorder the same cards. Learners explain the changed next-best alternative.

steps.teacher_says: Complete this sentence: I chose ___. My next-best option was ___, so my opportunity cost was ___.
steps.action: Ask pairs to explain rather than vote on a best activity.

activity.expected_reasoning: Opportunity cost depends on the specified next-best alternative, not the price or a moral judgment about the preference.
activity.scaffold: Use only two cards and a “choose / give up” mat before adding a third.
activity.extension: Give a time constraint rather than a money constraint; ask which extra information is needed if preferences are unknown.

printable_student_material.title: Choose one; name the next-best option
worksheet_prompts: For the fictional character, rank the options.

modules.title: Different baskets, different exposures
modules.goal: Explain why spreading exposure can reduce some concentration risks without guaranteeing profit.
modules.success_criterion: I can identify a shared exposure and explain what diversification can and cannot do.
modules.illustration_direction: Equal stacks of tokens in one restaurant basket versus several differently labeled sector baskets.

activity.title: What is in your baskets?
materials: Restaurant, technology, transport, and health sector cards

steps.teacher_says: Both portfolios start with eight tokens. Put all eight of A in restaurants. Split B equally among four sectors.
steps.action: Build equally valued portfolios with different exposures.

steps.teacher_says: A made-up event directly affects restaurants. Which tokens are exposed to this specific event?
steps.action: Mark the restaurant tokens; do not award invented returns or present the result as a real-market prediction.

steps.teacher_says: Now imagine an event affecting all sectors. Does spreading the tokens guarantee no loss?
steps.action: Discuss what protection was limited to the first event.

steps.teacher_says: Explain why four restaurant stocks can still share one kind of risk.
steps.action: Invite a comparison that refers to exposure, not merely card count.

activity.expected_reasoning: Different sectors can have different exposures. Diversification can reduce a particular concentration, while losses remain possible.
activity.scaffold: Use two sectors, clear labels, and the same number of tokens in both portfolios.
activity.extension: Ask why two companies from apparently different sectors might still share a supplier or other risk.

printable_student_material.title: Compare exposure
worksheet_prompts: Portfolio A: put eight tokens in restaurants.
Portfolio B: put two tokens in each sector.
Which portfolio has more direct exposure to a restaurant-only event? Why?
Why could both portfolios still lose value?

modules.title: Cash today, assets later
modules.goal: Distinguish total asset value from cash available for an immediate payment.
modules.success_criterion: I can compare available cash with a payment due before assets can be sold.
modules.illustration_direction: Two friendly trays labeled “Available today” and “Available later”, with banknotes and investment cards.

activity.title: Cash today, assets later
materials: Two trays/mats: Available today and Available later

steps.teacher_says: Maya has $200 cash and $700 in stocks. Leo has $400 cash and $500 in stocks. What is the same about their total value?
steps.action: Build both $900 positions with tokens on the two mats.

steps.teacher_says: A $300 payment is due today, before either can sell stocks. Which tokens can move to the payment area now?
steps.action: Use only tokens in Available today. Ask learners to explain the constraint.

steps.teacher_says: Does owning something valuable always mean you can spend that value immediately? What information would change the answer?
steps.action: Discuss timing of sale and payment without claiming cash is always best.

steps.teacher_says: A club owns equipment but has little cash. What would you check before saying it can pay a bill today?
steps.action: Connect the reasoning to a new fictional context, then offer the fresh check.

activity.expected_reasoning: Payment capacity depends on cash available at the deadline. Equal total assets can have different liquidity.
activity.scaffold: Provide pre-counted tokens and compare only the cash with the bill before discussing total assets.
activity.extension: Change the sale date or bill deadline and ask how this changes the conclusion; keep all sale values explicit.

printable_student_material.title: What can be used today?
scenario_cards: No stocks can be sold before payment.
worksheet_prompts: Maya can use ___ today. Leo can use ___ today.
Who can pay now? Explain using the deadline.
What new information could change the answer?

items.scenario: Sam can buy one stock now or keep the same money for a later purchase. Keeping the money is Sam’s next-best option. Sam chooses to buy the stock.
items.question: What is Sam’s opportunity cost?

answer_options.text: Keeping the money for the later purchase.
Only the number of dollars paid for the stock.
Every purchase Sam might ever make.
Any money the stock may earn.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: It is the next-best option Sam gives up by choosing the stock.
Opportunity cost always means the price paid.
Opportunity cost is every possible unchosen option added together.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The next-best alternative is explicitly keeping the money. Price is a monetary cost, but the concept asks which alternative is forgone.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: Ava can attend only one activity. Her first choice is library club, her second is football, and her third is watching a film. She chooses library club.
items.question: What is the opportunity cost of Ava’s choice?

answer_options.text: Both football and the film together.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: Football is Ava’s next-best alternative, which she gives up.
Opportunity cost is always the least preferred option.
The option chosen is also the opportunity cost.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The stated preference order identifies football as the next-best alternative. The film is another forgone option, but not the next-best one.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: In a simplified game choice, Noor can hold a stock or sell it now and use the money to buy another available stock. Selling and making that purchase is Noor’s next-best alternative. Noor holds.
items.question: Which opportunity does Noor give up?

answer_options.text: Selling now and using the money for the other stock.
The stock Noor continues to hold.
Only the price Noor originally paid.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: The opportunity cost is the stated next-best alternative to holding.
The opportunity cost is the option Noor selected.
Opportunity cost must include every imaginable future option.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The alternative forgone is explicitly specified. There is no claim that holding or selling will produce a better return.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: A class has $20 and can buy either a book set or an art kit, each costing $20. The class prefers the book set, and the art kit is its next-best option. The class buys the books.
items.question: What is the opportunity cost?

answer_options.text: The books and art kit together.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: The art kit is the next-best alternative given up.
Opportunity cost is what the class bought.
Every option is an opportunity cost even if it was chosen.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The preference and resource constraint make the forgone next-best option clear.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: Two portfolios have the same total value. Portfolio A holds only restaurant companies. Portfolio B holds companies in several different sectors. An event directly harms restaurant companies. Nothing else about returns is given.
items.question: Which portfolio has more of its value directly exposed to this restaurant event?

answer_options.text: They must have exactly the same exposure.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: All of A is in the affected sector; B spreads some exposure across other sectors.
Any portfolio with several stock cards cannot lose money.
All sectors are always affected in exactly the same way.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: A has more direct sector concentration. This does not predict exact returns or guarantee that B will profit.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: One fictional class business puts its whole budget into lemonade. Another splits an equal budget across lemonade, bookmarks, and crafts. The lemon supplier cannot deliver. Other supplies are unaffected.
items.question: Which business has more of its budget directly exposed to the missing lemons?

answer_options.text: The business split across three products.
Both must lose all their money.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: The lemonade-only business concentrates its budget in the affected product.
Splitting a budget guarantees no losses.
If one part has a problem, every other part must have the identical problem.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The event explicitly affects the lemon supply alone. Spreading exposure can limit this direct concentration without eliminating all business risk.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: Mina has four stocks, all in restaurant companies. Jay has four stocks spread across four different sectors. Values are equal. A disruption specifically affects restaurant companies.
items.question: Whose portfolio is more directly concentrated in the affected sector?

answer_options.text: Neither, because four cards always means diversification.
Both are guaranteed to make money.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: Different exposures matter; Mina’s four stocks share restaurant-sector risk.
The number of cards alone determines diversification.
Owning several stocks guarantees profit.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: Equal card counts do not imply equally varied exposure.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: A friend says: “I spread my money across three different businesses, so I cannot lose money.”
items.question: Which reply is most accurate?

answer_options.text: Spreading exposure may reduce some risks, but losses are still possible.
The friend is right: several businesses guarantee no loss.
Only one business can ever lose money.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: Some events can affect several businesses, and each business still has risks.
The number three guarantees a safe investment.
Spreading money changes uncertain returns into promised returns.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: Diversification is a risk-management idea, not a promise of profit or protection from every loss.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: Maya has $200 cash and stocks worth $700. Leo has $400 cash and stocks worth $500. Each must pay $300 today. Neither can sell stocks before the payment is due.
items.question: Who can pay immediately from available cash?
items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: Leo has at least $300 cash today; Maya has only $200 available today.
Both have $900 in total assets, so all of it is available to pay today.
Maya’s higher stock value means Maya must have more available cash.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: Equal total asset value does not imply equal liquidity at the payment deadline. The sale constraint is part of the fictional scenario, not a universal game or real-market rule.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: A school club has $25 cash and equipment worth $200. A $40 bill is due today. The club cannot sell equipment until next month and has no other funds.
items.question: Can the club pay the full bill today?

answer_options.text: No, it has only $25 available today.
Yes, because equipment is always the same as cash.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: The equipment cannot supply cash before the bill is due.
Owning assets worth more than a bill always means being able to pay immediately.
$25 is greater than $40.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The club is $15 short in available cash. The numerical distractor should trigger a calculation check, not automatically a liquidity misconception.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: In a simplified scenario, Eli starts with $600 cash and buys an asset for $450. A $200 expense is then due before Eli can sell any assets. No other cash arrives.
items.question: Can Eli cover the expense from remaining cash?

answer_options.text: No; $150 remains, which is less than $200.
Yes; the asset is still worth $450.
Yes; any asset can always be sold before a payment.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: The purchase leaves $150 available before the payment deadline.
The asset’s value can automatically be spent as cash.
$600 minus $450 equals $250.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: Remaining cash is $150. The problem specifies no sale before payment. Separate subtraction errors from reasoning about accessible assets.

items.access_support: Teacher may read the prompt aloud without explaining the concept. Record supports used consistently.

items.scenario: Alex has $60 cash and collectibles worth $140. Quinn has $120 cash and collectibles worth $80. Each owes $100 today. Neither can sell collectibles until next week.
items.question: Who can pay today from available cash?

answer_options.text: Both, because each has $200 in assets.

items.reason_prompt: Which reason best explains your answer?

reason_options.text: Quinn has $120 available today; Alex has $60 available today.
All assets are immediately usable as cash.
More collectible value always means more available cash.
I am not sure.

teacher_only.rationale: The difference is timing and form of assets, not total asset value.

suggestion_rules.opportunity-cost: Map concept-specific opportunity-cost reason tags to activity-next-best.
suggestion_rules.diversification: Map concept-specific exposure/guarantee reason tags to activity-different-baskets.
suggestion_rules.liquidity: Map assets/cash-availability reason tags to activity-cash-today.

suggestion_rules.uncertain: Gather more evidence or invite an explanation; do not infer a specific misconception.
